cues.text: The Gospel of John tells us that Andrew , a fisherman from Bethsaida on the Sea of Galilee, was originally a disciple of John the Baptist , standing alongside his teacher when John pointed toward Jesus passing by and declared him the Lamb of God.

Andrew and another disciple immediately followed Jesus, remaining with him for the rest of that day — a first encounter significant enough that Eastern Christian tradition has long given Andrew the title Protokletos , "the First-Called," honoring him as the very first of the future Twelve to become Christ's disciple.

Andrew's first recorded action after this encounter reveals, in miniature, the whole pattern of his discipleship: he went at once to find his own brother, Simon , and announced to him, "we have found the Messiah," bringing Simon directly to Jesus, who would soon give him the new name Peter — the rock on which the Church would be built.

Throughout the Gospels, Andrew appears less often as a central figure than as a quiet connector, repeatedly bringing others into Christ's presence: it is Andrew who points out the boy with five barley loaves and two fish before the miraculous feeding of the five thousand, and Andrew, together with Philip , who brings a group of Greek visitors seeking an audience with Jesus during his final days in Jerusalem.

Though the Gospels give Andrew fewer individual scenes than his brother Peter or the sons of Zebedee, he is consistently numbered among the first four disciples named in every listing of the Twelve, and appears among the small group of Apostles Jesus draws closer to himself on certain significant occasions, such as the private teaching on the Mount of Olives concerning the end times — evidence that, however quietly he moves through the Gospel narrative, Andrew's place among Christ's closest followers was never in doubt.
Carrying the Gospel North and East

According to ancient and widespread tradition, after Pentecost Andrew carried the Gospel into the regions north and east of the Black Sea, through Asia Minor, Thrace, and into Scythia — territories that would, many centuries later, become Georgia, Ukraine, and Russia, all of which honor Andrew today as a patron of their lands, alongside Scotland, whose own association with the Apostle traces to medieval relic traditions and to Andrew's continuing status as its national patron saint.
A Cross He Deemed Himself Unworthy to Share

Tradition holds that Andrew's missionary journeys eventually brought him to Patras in Greece, where his preaching provoked the hostility of the Roman governor, and where he was condemned to death by crucifixion.

According to the same tradition, Andrew, out of profound humility, asked that he not be crucified on a cross of the same shape as his Lord's, considering himself unworthy of so close an identification with Christ's own death — a request later tradition connected to the distinctive X-shaped "saltire" cross that has borne his name on flags, emblems, and in religious art ever since — though the X-shape itself is a medieval addition, first clearly attested in Scottish heraldry around 1286, and appears nowhere in the earliest accounts of his martyrdom.

Andrew died, by tradition, around AD 60, bound rather than nailed to his cross so that his suffering, and his preaching to the crowds gathered to watch, might be prolonged for several days before his death.

Honored as the patron of Scotland, Russia, Ukraine, Georgia, Romania, and the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople alike, Andrew — the quiet connector who was always bringing someone else to Christ, from his own brother to a boy's small lunch to a group of curious strangers — remains a model for every believer whose truest calling may be, simply and repeatedly, to introduce others to the One he himself was the very first to follow.

His feast, kept close to the beginning of Advent each year, fittingly reminds the whole Church, at the very start of a new liturgical year, that the entire Christian life begins with the same single, decisive step Andrew took by the Jordan: to leave what we know and follow.
